entities.name: Eunomius of Cyzicus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Eunomius of Cyzicus (born early 4th century CE in Dacora, Cappadocia, or Corniaspa, Pontus; died 394 CE) emerged as the most intellectually formidable and uncompromising leader of the Anomoean Arian faction within the tumultuous Christological debates of the 4th-century Roman Empire. His radical theological stance, asserting the absolute dissimilarity (anomoios) between God the Father and God the Son, directly challenged the Nicene orthodoxy establishing the Son's co-equality and co-eternity with the Father. Eunomius's rigorous dialectic and influential writings profoundly shaped the trajectory of Arianism, provoking strong counter-responses from prominent Nicene theologians like Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa, and contributing significantly to the theological polarization that defined late Roman Christianity.

His ecclesiastical career was marked by rapid ascent and recurrent exile. Ordained deacon by Aetius, another prominent Anomoean, Eunomius quickly gained renown for his sharp intellect and persuasive rhetoric. He served briefly as Bishop of Cyzicus around 360 CE, appointed by the Arian-sympathetic Emperor Constantius II, but was swiftly deposed due to local opposition and his own controversial teachings. Subsequent periods saw him at Constantinople, where he engaged in public theological disputations, and in various places of exile, including Cappadocia and Mauritania, reflecting the shifting imperial policies towards religious dissent. His most significant works, including his Apology and Apologia Apologiae, systematically articulated his Anomoean Christology, arguing that the divine essence of the Father was utterly unbegotten and therefore incommunicable to the Son, who was a created being.
